segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I make known to you, brothers and sisters, the good news that I announced to you, which you also received, in which you also stand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and through which you are also being saved, if you hold fast to the message with which I announced the good news to you—unless you believed in vain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I handed on to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After that he appeared to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, most of whom remain until now, though some have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After that he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Last of all, as if to a miscarried child, he appeared to me as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am the least of the apostles, not fit to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me did not prove empty; on the contrary, I labored harder than all of them—though not I, but the grace of God that is with me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So whether it was I or they, this is what we proclaim and this is what you believed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if Christ is proclaimed as having been raised from the dead, how can some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised either;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation is empty, and your faith is empty too.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are also found to be false witnesses about God, because we testified against God that he raised Christ—whom he did not raise, if in fact the dead are not raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if the dead are not raised, then Christ has not been raised either;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have also perished.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If our hope in Christ is for this life only, we are more to be pitied than all other people.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For since death came through a human, the resurrection of the dead has also come through a human.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But each in the proper order: Christ the firstfruits; then, at his coming, those who belong to Christ;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every rule and every authority and power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he must reign until he has put all enemies under his feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The last enemy to be abolished is death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “he has subjected all things under his feet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when it says that all things have been subjected, it is clear that this excludes the one who subjected all things to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Otherwise, what will those people do who are baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized on their behalf?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And why do we ourselves face danger every hour?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I die every day—I swear it by my boasting in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus from merely human motives, what good is that to me? If the dead are not raised,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be led astray: “Bad company ruins good character.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sober up, as you rightly should, and stop sinning; for some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But someone will say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Fool! What you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as for what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of something else.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each of the seeds its own body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not all flesh is the same flesh: there is one for humans, another flesh for animals, another flesh for birds, and another for fish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but the glory of the heavenly is one kind, and that of the earthly is another.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sun has one glory, the moon another glory, and the stars another glory; for star differs from star in glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So it is with the resurrection of the dead. It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So also it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The first human, Adam, became a living being”;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the spiritual is not first; the natural is, and then the spiritual.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first human was from the earth, made of dust; the second human is from heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the one made of dust was, so also are those made of dust; and as the heavenly one is, so also are the heavenly ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And just as we have borne the image of the one made of dust, we will also bear the image of the heavenly one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What I am saying, brothers and sisters, is this: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, I am telling you a secret: we will not all fall asleep, but we will all be changed,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in an instant, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this perishable body must put on imperishability, and this mortal body must put on immortality.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when this perishable body has put on imperishability and this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Where, death, is your victory? Where, death, is your sting?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my beloved brothers and sisters, be steadfast, immovable, always overflowing in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not empty.

notes.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two; the related verb in verses 1 and 2 is rendered “announced” with “good news.”

The Greek word denotes a miscarriage or stillbirth, as in the Greek versions of Numbers 12:12 and Job 3:16; it does not mean a late birth. Most translations soften it to “one untimely born” or “abnormally born.” What Paul intends by the image is debated: it may be a term of abuse he is taking over from critics, or a picture of the violent and irregular way he became an apostle.

A first-century hearer knew this word as the term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s word for Israel assembled. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

notes.traditional: If in this life only we have hope in Christ
notes.note: The word “only” stands at the end of the Greek clause. It may limit “in this life,” as rendered here and in most translations, or it may qualify the whole clause: “if in this life we have done nothing more than hope in Christ.” Either way the point is that a hope with no resurrection behind it is pitiable.

The Greek word means a human being, not specifically a male, and Paul’s argument turns on Adam and Christ each standing for humanity. The same rendering is kept in verses 45 and 47, where translations traditionally have “the first man” and “the second man.” Some recent versions likewise use “human being” here.

The Greek word means arrival and presence. In Paul’s world it was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, and a first-century reader would have heard that royal overtone here.

Many translations have “destroyed” here and in verse 26. The Greek verb is not the ordinary word for destroying; it means to put out of operation or bring to an end, and the lexicons give “abolish” among its senses. The same English word is used in both verses so that the repetition is heard.

notes.phrase: baptized on behalf of the dead
notes.note: The plain sense of the Greek is that some people were being baptized on behalf of people who had died, and most scholars read it that way, though nothing else is known of such a practice in Paul’s time. Many other explanations have been proposed and none has won general agreement. Paul neither commends nor condemns the practice; he appeals to it only as evidence that those who do it expect the dead to be raised.

The verb is the term for fighting animals in the arena. Most scholars take it here as a figure for violent human opposition in Ephesus, since Paul gives no hint elsewhere of having survived the arena, but a literal sense cannot be ruled out. The saying that closes the verse is from Isaiah 22:13.
This is a line of Greek verse, usually attributed to the comic playwright Menander, which by Paul’s time circulated as a proverb. The word rendered “company” can also mean “conversation.”

“Natural” and “spiritual” translate adjectives formed from the Greek words for the life of a living creature and for spirit, the same pair that appears in verse 45 as “living being” and “life-giving spirit.” Most scholars hold that the contrast is between a body animated by ordinary life and a body animated by the Spirit, not between a material body and an immaterial one. English cannot show the verbal link, so the traditional pair is kept. The quotation in verse 45 is Genesis 2:7, to which Paul adds “first” and “Adam.”

Many early and important manuscripts read “let us also bear,” an exhortation, which differs from “we will also bear” by a single vowel that was pronounced alike. The Greek text followed here prints the future, as do most modern translations, on the ground that the passage is describing what will happen, not urging conduct. A number of scholars prefer the better-attested exhortation.

In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. Most English versions keep “mystery” as an established term for a truth once hidden and now revealed. “Secret” is used here because “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas Paul goes straight on to state the matter plainly.

candidates.reason: The plural as an address to mixed congregations occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so one policy is needed.
It recurs in 1 Corinthians 2:14, James 3:15 and Jude 19 in contrast with “spiritual,” and versions vary between “natural,” “physical,” “unspiritual” and “worldly.”
The sleep metaphor for death recurs in the Gospels, Acts, Paul and 2 Peter, and some versions flatten it to “die,” so a single decision on keeping the image is needed.
It is used of cosmic subjection, civil authorities and household relations, where versions vary between “subject,” “submit” and “be subordinate,” and readers would be misled by unexplained variation.
The φθορά/ἀφθαρσία word-group recurs in Romans, Galatians, Ephesians, 1–2 Peter and elsewhere, and “corruption,” “decay” and “perishable” give different impressions of physical versus moral ruin.
